data.biography:
Dr. Abdul Rasheed, alias Nokap Baloch, was killed on the morning of 11 September 2026 at his residence in the Shamsar Hakabad area of Western Balochistan, in Iranian-occupied Balochistan.

According to an eyewitness, two armed men associated with a death squad arrived at Dr. Abdul Rasheed’s guest house while posing as patients. The eyewitness stated that the assailants subsequently opened fire on Dr. Abdul Rasheed, killing him. According to BNM, the individuals were linked to a death squad operating under the supervision of the Pakistani Army.

Dr. Abdul Rasheed’s killing represents the loss of a dedicated doctor, educator, political activist, and community worker who devoted his life to serving vulnerable and displaced communities. Despite experiencing displacement and repeated threats to his own life, he remained committed to providing essential medical care, education, and humanitarian assistance to people in need, particularly those facing hardship and limited access to basic services.

Dr. Abdul Rasheed Baloch, alias Nokaap Baloch, was born in 1982 in the home of Ghulam Hussain in Gandachai, Kolowah, Awaran. From an early age, he pursued his education and developed a strong commitment to education and public service.

In his birthplace of Gandachai and the surrounding areas of Kolowah, many people faced a shortage of teachers. In response, Dr. Abdul Rasheed supported community efforts to arrange for teachers and personally taught children on a voluntary basis for several years in the nearby village of Kenechi.

After completing his education, he continued to serve his community by providing free medical treatment. His work as a doctor and educator remained an important part of his life, alongside his political and organisational activities.

According to information provided by Dr. Nokaap’s family, he had previously faced reprisals allegedly linked to his political activities and public role in Kolowah.

In 2016, his home was demolished during a military operation, and his property was looted by the Pakistani Army. The family also reported that attempts had been made to kill him. As threats to his life and insecurity continued, Dr. Abdul Rasheed was ultimately forced to leave his home in 2018 and relocate to Western Balochistan.

Displacement did not end his commitment to his community. Despite being forced to leave his home, Dr. Abdul Rasheed continued his medical, educational, social, and political activities and remained committed to supporting people in need.

On 21 October 2025, a statement was issued by Baloch Khan, the spokesperson of the Baloch Raaji Aajoi Sangar (BRAS), an umbrella alliance of Baloch armed organizations. The statement said that, in defence of the Baloch population in Zehri, Khuzdar, Balochistan, BRAS forces eliminated dozens of enemy personnel, while six freedom fighters embraced martyrdom. Among them was Sanaullah Baloch, alias Baty Khan

The statement added that the occupying Pakistani army attempted to advance for aggressive purposes in the Zehri area of Khuzdar, which is under the control of the Baloch Raaji Ajoi Sangar (BRAS), resulting in fierce clashes. Dozens of occupying army personnel were eliminated in these clashes, while six freedom fighters of the Baloch Raaji Aajoi Sangar were martyred in defence of the motherland.

Among the martyrs, Abdul Aziz Baloch and Hafiz Muhammad Umar Baloch were martyred on 26 September, while Sanaullah Baloch, Abdul Aziz Baloch, Rashid Ahmed Zehri, and Fiaz Jattak were martyred on 30 September.

Martyr Sanaullah Baloch alias Baty Khan, son of Pir Wali Bhatar, belonged to Zehri, Khuzdar, Balochistan He joined Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) four months ago. In a short period of time, he gained prominence with his intelligence, passion and military skills. As an urban guerrilla he played a key role in monitoring enemy movements, intelligence networks and ground defense. Till his last breath, he bravely fought the enemy in defense of motherland.

On 9 November 2026, a statement issued by Baloch Republican Guards spokesperson Dostain Baloch announced the martyrdom of five members of the organisation and paid red salutes to them.

The spokesperson said: “We pay heartfelt tribute and offer red salutes to the sincere, brave, and ideologically committed fighters of the Baloch Republican Guards: Commander Habibullah Jan Jatoi, alias Laghari; Sharif Jatoi, alias Commando; Saeed Jan Jatoi, alias Nana; Hazrat Jatoi, alias Bolani; and Umeed Ali Jatoi, alias Nadir. They embraced martyrdom while bravely fighting against the occupying Pakistani army in the Sanni area of Kachhi for the freedom and right to self-determination of Balochistan."

On 1 November 2026, in the Sanni area of Kachhi, Commander Habibullah Jan and his revolutionary comrades launched an ambush against a convoy of the occupying Pakistani army.
Commander Habibullah Jan and his brave fighters fiercely engaged the enemy on the front lines, inflicting significant human and material losses on the occupying forces.
During the clash, an enemy drone suddenly launched an attack, seriously injuring Commander Habibullah Jan, Saeed, Hazrat, and Umeed. Despite their injuries, they continued to face the consequences of the attack. However, unable to survive their severe injuries, Habibullah Jan and his comrades later embraced martyrdom. All five members were residents of the Sanni area of Kachhi.

To sabotage the Baloch National Gathering in the coastal city of Gwadar and to stop the peaceful caravan marching toward it, Pakistani forces opened indiscriminate fire on peaceful protesters in the Talaar area of Mastung on July 27, 2024, martyring Naseer Langove.

Safar Khan, son of Haji Fateh Muhammad, was a 31-year-old farmer from Kohda Kohdask, Khuzdar. On 3 March 2026, he was forcibly disappeared by Pakistan’s Frontier Corps in Basima, Washuk, Balochistan.
For six agonising months, his family waited for his return. They waited for a knock on the door, a phone call, or any sign that Safar was still alive. Instead, on 17 September 2026, his body was found dumped at Mashkai Cross, Balochistan.

A statement issued by the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) spokesperson, Jeeyand Baloch, said that an important member of the organization, Lal Mohammed Marri, alias Lalu, lost his life and embraced martyrdom on 23 March 2019 in an accident while carrying out an important mission.
Lal Mohammed had been affiliated with the BLA’s Bolan Front since 2015, and due to his intelligence and bravery, he quickly became a prominent member of the organization. He participated in many successful combats against the enemy and played a significant role. Jeeyand Baloch said that the BLA respects and values the national service and immortal role of Martyr Lal Mohammed Marri and pays rich tributes to him. He is a role model for Baloch youth.

Mehboob Wadhela, a leader of the Baloch National Movement, was abducted and forcibly disappeared by Pakistani forces on April 3, 2010. His mutilated body, along with the mutilated body of Baloch Republican Party senior leader Abdul Rehman Arif, was found in Ormara on February 23, 2011.

On 29th December 2025, the Pakistani forces Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) abducted and forcibly disappeared 24 year old student Hamdan, son of Mohammad Ali, a resident of Mangopir, Purana Golimar, Karachi, from Duhbi Goth, Golimar, Karachi.
After 50 days in custody, on 17th February 2026, the CTD announced that Hamdan was among several individuals killed during an armed encounter in Shah Latif Town, Karachi. Authorities claimed that the deceased were militants who died in an exchange of fire. However, Hamdan had already been in the custody of Pakistani forces since his abduction in December 2025.

On 17 November 2024, a statement issued by Balochistan Liberation Army spokesperson Azad Baloch stated that on 25 February 2024, three members of the BLA - Mohammad Deen alias Chakar Bolani, Shoaib Shahwani alias Riaz Baloch, and Asim Kurd alias Nazir Baloch - were killed in an attack by death squads in Kahan, district Kohlu, Balochistan.
The three comrades were returning to their frontlines after completing a special organizational mission in Kahan when operatives of a death squad, lying in ambush, opened fire on them. As a result, all three members of the organization were killed.
Asim Kurd alias Nazir Baloch, son of Panah Khan Kurd, was from Saryab Chiltan Gali in Quetta. Both joined the BLA in 2023. After briefly serving in Quetta, they left civilian life to join the mountainous frontlines. In just eight months, they contributed to the national cause in Koh-e-Dungan, Bolan, Kahan, and other fronts.

On December 14, 2024 three brave BLA fighters were martyred in SabzKoh, Panjgur, while valiantly resisting a Pakistani military offensive. That morning, Pakistani forces launched a large-scale air and ground operation, deploying hundreds of troops, SSG commandos, gunship helicopters, and drones. At SabzKoh, BLA fighters engaged in an intense battle from 10 AM to 3 PM. Commander Majeed Baloch, Commander Diljan Baloch, and fighter Zakir Jan fought courageously before embracing martyrdom.
Zakir Jan Baloch, alias Lakmeer Baloch, was originally from Pasni. He joined the organization a year before his martyrdom and began his struggle from the Panjgur front. In this short period, through his relentless hard work, sincerity, and bravery, he proved himself to be an outstanding freedom fighter in every aspect. The organization will always honor his struggle and sacrifice.

Munir Ahmad, son of Babu Jalaluddin, was a 33-year-old farmer from Kohda, a resident of Kohdask, Khuzdar. On 18 February 2026, he was forcibly disappeared by the Frontier Corps of the Pakistani forces in Basima, Washuk. For seven months, his family lived with the pain and uncertainty of his enforced disappearance. On 17 September 2026, their wait ended with the discovery of Munir Ahmad’s dead body, dumped at Mashkai Cross.
Munir Ahmad was a farmer who worked in his fields to provide for his family. He belonged to a poor family and lived with the dignity of his labour. His family needed their son, not his dead body.
A man who left home to work in his fields was forcibly disappeared and, seven months later, returned to his family only as a body.

At 5:00 AM on 31 January 2026, Jeeyand Baloch, spokesperson for the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), issued a statement announcing the commencement of the second phase of Operation Herof against the occupying state and its military and administrative structures. The operation remained active for six days, concluding at 4:00 PM on 6 February 2026.
On 6 February 2026, a concluding statement by the spokesperson declared that Operation Herof Phase 2 had concluded in a decisive victory across all fronts. It stated that Operation Herof Phase 2, carried out by the Baloch Liberation Army, was a six-day campaign of coordinated urban combat and represented the most extensive, intense, and organized military engagement in the modern history of the Baloch national resistance. The operation, which began at 5:00 AM on 31 January and ended at 4:00 PM on 6 February, successfully achieved its strategic objectives. Fourteen cities across Balochistan were targeted. Baloch fighters launched simultaneous attacks and established effective control over numerous enemy posts, military installations, and urban sectors. In several cities, BLA units maintained uninterrupted dominance over occupying forces for six consecutive days, inflicting significant political, psychological, and military damage on the enemy.
During the operation, 93 BLA fighters were martyred. These included 50 fidayeen from the Majeed Brigade, 26 fighters from the Fateh Squad, and 17 from the Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS). All major BLA units participated in the operation, including Majeed Brigade, STOS, Fateh Squad, ZIRAB (intelligence wing), and Hakkal (media wing). Over 362 enemy personnel were killed, including members of the Pakistani Army, Frontier Corps, police, and state-sponsored death squads. Seventeen enemy soldiers were captured. Ten, identified as Baloch, were released with warnings, while seven remained in BLA custody and faced trial for war crimes and acts of genocide.
On 14 February 2026, another statement by the spokesperson announced that the seven occupying army personnel were in custody and that a one-week prison of war exchange had been offered. The Pakistani Army ignored the offer and intensified its military operations. On 3 March 2026, a subsequent statement declared that, due to misadventures and breaches of promises by the occupying forces, death sentences were carried out against the seven Pakistani personnel.
During Operation Herof Phase 2, dozens of Pakistani military facilities were destroyed, weapons stockpiles were seized, and the unified, disciplined resistance dealt a substantial blow to the military superiority of the occupying state.
Nisar Baloch, alias Zadag, son of Noor Bano was resident of Killi Jamaldini area of Noshki District Balochistan and joined the BLA on 2020 and joined the Majeed Brigade December 2020 and he served in Bolan, Noshki fronts as Operation Command Rank.
Nisar Baloch was an experienced Sarmachar (Freedom Fighter) who served on the Bolan and Noshki fronts. After joining the BLA in 2020, he volunteered for the Majeed Brigade. He was a mature and highly capable fighter. On the Bolan and Noshki fronts, he led numerous combats. He possessed an exceptional ability to organize the ranks of his fellow Sarmachars, make decisions under pressure, and anticipate the enemy’s moves in advance. His orders were brief yet decisive, and his presence on the battlefield created strong discipline and confidence. On this principle, he continued to advance his units and played an effective role in every combat.
Alongside this, he was also a revolutionary poet whose words resonated in hearts like the echo of gunpowder. His poetry was not merely an emotional expression but a conscious declaration of resistance that re-energized fighters and renewed morale. He kept the pen alive even in the trench and raised the message of resistance from the battlefield. Thus, he emerged as a soldier of both the gun and the word, proving that in revolutionary struggle, thought and warfare reinforce one another.
Nisar Baloch also participated in Operation Dara-e-Bolan Phase I, Phase II, and Operation Herof Phase I. In Operation Herof Phase II, he served as the operation commander of the Noshki FC Headquarters front, where his leadership placed enemy forces under intense psychological pressure, the enemy forces had conceded defeat even before engaging in combat. As a result, during the six-day battle of Noshki, the Sarmachars maintained control of the entire city, and after achieving all military and political objectives of Operation Herof, they withdrew from the city in an organized manner.
Nisar Baloch embraced martyrdom on the Noshki front, inscribing his name among the martyrs of the war of freedom and becoming immortal.

In 1838, the British sent a force led by Alexander Burnes to reinstate Shah Shuja Durrani as the king of Afghanistan by deposing Amir Dost Mohammad Khan. To reach Afghanistan, they needed passage through Balochistan, particularly the Bolan Pass. However, Khan Mehrab Khan refused to allow the British to use his land to attack a neighboring country. The British sent Lieutenant Leach to negotiate with the Baloch government, but the Khan stood firm. When British forces reached Shaal via Bolan, some patriotic Baloch, without the Khan’s knowledge, attacked British troops out of nationalist sentiment and a desire to protect their homeland.
After toppling Amir Dost Mohammad Khan, the British Governor General of India, Lord Auckland, ordered an attack on Balochistan. In 1839, around 7,000 British troops marched from Shaal to attack the Baloch Meeri (capital). Anticipating an invasion, Khan Mehrab Khan declared war and sent messages to tribal leaders, but many saw the British as allies rather than invaders and chose to collaborate with them rather than defend their land. When Khan Mehrab Khan gathered his resistance fighters, the number of loyal warriors had dwindled to only 700 due to the short sightedness of many tribal chiefs. Nevertheless, Mehrab Khan was determined to fight. At his court, a respected figure, Akhund Muhammad Siddiq, advised him that he was not in a position to wage war at that time. He suggested that the Khan should leave Kalat with his companions, regroup and strengthen his forces, and then launch an attack against the British when the time was right, on 13 November 1839, the British forces launched an attack on Kalat, and a fierce battle ensued. During the fighting, Khan Mehrab Khan Baloch was martyred by a British bullet.

Among those martyred alongside him were:

Diwan Bacha Mal, Minister of Finance

Diwan Khem Chand

Diwan Asardas Mukhi, from the Hindu Panchayat of Kalat

Abdul Karim Raisani, brother of Sardar Asad Khan Raisani

Sardar Wali Muhammad Shahizai Mengal, (maternal uncle of Martyr Amir Mehrab Khan)

Mir Taj Muhammad Shahizai Mengal, (cousin of Mehrab Khan)

Mir Muhammad Ali Shahizai Mengal

Mir Fazal Muhammad Lehri, brother of Sardar Muhammad Khan Lehri

Sardar Zaman Khan Pandrani

Mir Dad Karim Chandozai Shahwani

Mir Shahbaz Khan Nichari

Mir Badal Khan, brother of Sardar Shahbaz Khan Nichari

Khan Muhammad Dehwaar, Arbab-e-Kalat.

Mir Nabi Bakhsh Jatoi, from the Narmak region of Kalat

Mir Qaiser Khan Bizenjo

Mir Shah Dost Bizenjo

Muhammad Raza Waziri Khel

Noor Muhammad Shahizai, son of Polat Sagaar Sarmastani, in charge of the armory

Taj Muhammad Shagasi

On 31 December 2025, a statement released by the spokesperson of the Balochistan Liberation Front, Major Gwahram Baloch, stated that five of its fighters embraced martyrdom and sacrificed their lives for the homeland in an enemy drone strike in Kalat on 25 December 2025.
The martyrs include Abdul Ahad Dehwar alias Gazzain, son of Hamayun Dehwar, resident of Keli Kahriz Mastung; Israr Ahmad alias Ibrar, son of Hussain, resident of Gargina Mastung; Shoaib Ahmad alias Subedar, son of Muhammad Ali, resident of Jiwa Khuzdar; Obaidullah Siyahpad alias Sabzu, son of Peerjan, resident of Kharan; and Faisal Badini alias Qazi, son of Muhammad Ibrahim, resident of Kharan.
Israr Ahmad alias Ibrar, son of Hussain, joined the Balochistan Liberation Front in August 2025 and initially performed responsibilities in the organization’s intelligence wing in the city with steadfastness and sincerity, in accordance with organizational directives. He was martyred in the drone strike in Kalat on 25 December 2025.

On the morning of January 8, 2026, at around 10 AM in the Zamuran area of Buleda, the Pakistani military carried out a drone attack on the Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) camp, resulting in the martyrdom of four BLF fighters. The martyrs include Hussain, alias Kamal Baloch; Akbar, alias Tahir Baloch; Waseem, alias Mero Baloch; and Huzaifa, alias Nodan Baloch.
Akbar, alias Tahir Baloch, son of Yaqoob and resident of Buleda Menaz, joined the BLF on March 13, 2025. He had recently arrived at the organization’s camp and was active in its urban operations. Despite his short time at the camp, he became a model for every fighter through his bravery, hard work, and dedication. He carried out every responsibility with complete commitment and sincerity and played an active role on multiple fronts. The BLF will always honor his sacrifice and dedication.

Martyr Jalil Sher Baloch, alias Kambar Baloch, was born in the house of Sher Mohammad Baloch in the Hoshab area of Kech, Balochistan. He began his political journey on the platform of the Baloch Students Organization (BSO Azad). In 2009, he joined the pro-independence armed organization, the Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF), and in 2014, he joined the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA). Until his last breath, he remained engaged in his organizational activities, striving to do his best to advance the caravan of the Baloch liberation movement.
He embraced martyrdom along with eight comrades - Kambar Baloch, Samad Baloch, Dad Shah, Shoaib Baloch, Rahmdil Baloch, Haris Baloch, and Nawaz Baloch - in a drone attack by the Pakistan Army on November 29, 2022, in the Jath, Kolwa area of Kech, Balochistan.

On 22 July 2025, around 9:00 AM, in the Kohak area of Kalat, the Pakistani army attempted an aggressive advance, which was targeted by Sarmachars (BLA fighters) through an ambush. The attack lasted for more than forty minutes, during which nine personnel of the occupying Pakistani army were killed on the spot, while several others fled in injured condition.
For the past five days, the occupying forces have been trying to advance in Kohak and surrounding areas, but due to the strong strategy of the Baloch Liberation Army’s Sarmachars, the occupying army has continuously suffered heavy losses. In these same clashes, Sohaib Baloch alias Ameer Bakhsh attained the rank of martyrdom.
Martyr Sangat Sohaib Baloch alias Ameer Bakhsh, son of Muhammad Deen, originally belonged to the Manguchar area of Kalat and was residing in Kali Ismail, Quetta at the time. He had joined the Baloch Liberation Army a year ago and was rendering services on the Kalat front for the achievement of national freedom.
Martyr Sohaib Baloch was a brave, courageous, and principled comrade who participated in several important operations during his short but determined revolutionary life. He was not only a valiant soldier but also a conscious revolutionary activist whose commitment to the movement’s ideology remained unwavering.
In his final battle as well, he remained on the front line, delivering heavy blows to the occupying army and inflicting severe losses on the enemy. His bravery and sacrifice serve as a shining example not only for the Kalat front but for the entire national movement.
Fareed Khan Baloch, was a resident of the Anjira, Khuzdar area of Balochistan. He was martyred on 2 July 2012 in Balochistan.

Mohammad Ashraf Mengal, alias Sarbuland, son of Abdul Rahman Mengal, was a resident of the Pandran area of District Kalat, Balochistan. He joined the BLA in 2025 and had been active in Kalat against the Pakistani genocidal forces. He was martyred on the Noshki front during Operation Herof Phase 2.
Muhammad Ashraf Mengal, named “Sarbuland” (The High-Headed) by his comrades for his unwavering courage, was a custodian of the rugged mountains and honorable traditions of Kalat. His journey of resistance was not merely born of impulse but was a response to the years of tyranny endured by his family. Sarbuland’s entire family was targeted under the draconian policy of “collective punishment”; his elderly father and brothers were forcibly disappeared, an ordeal that transformed Ashraf’s longing for freedom into an unquenchable flame. Instead of breaking him, the separation from his loved ones and the hardships of the dungeons fortified his resolve, leading him to choose the path of armed struggle in 2025.
On the arduous fronts of Kalat, Sarbuland proved his military prowess. He was a warrior whose heart carried not the fire of blind revenge, but the light of love for his motherland. When Operation Herof commenced, he chose to face death head-on at the Noshki front. During the intense clashes, he proved that a nation whose youth are driven toward the battlefield rather than intimidated by torture cells is impossible to subjugate. Muhammad Ashraf Mengal embraced martyrdom while fighting the enemy until his last breath, living up to his name by holding his nation’s head high.

Ayaz Baloch, son of Khuda Rahim, was a 26 year old cleaner at a government school from the Tasp area of Panjgur district in Balochistan.
On 30 April 2026, Ayaz Baloch was targeted and killed by a Pakistani state forces death squad in Nokabad, Tasp, near his home at around 9:30 PM.

On 12 August 2026, Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) spokesperson Gwahran Baloch issued a statement announcing the martyrdom of nine fighters of the organization: 1. Zubair Baloch, alias Shahvez; 2. Shahnawaz Baloch, alias Rahchar; 3. Rahim Baloch, alias Ajiz Baloch; 4. Musharaf Baloch, alias Basham; 5. Munir Baloch, alias Khalid Baloch; 6. Mohammad Zaman, alias Yahya; 7. Jasim Baloch, alias Babar; 8. Gaji Khan Baloch, alias Aftab; and 9. Abdullah Baloch, alias Usman, and paid tribute to all the martyred comrades who sacrificed their lives for the freedom of the motherland, Balochistan.

On 23 July 2026, amidst the ongoing struggle for the defence and liberation of the motherland, BLF fighters were patrolling the Mand area to carry out routine organisational duties when they encountered a blockade set up by the occupying forces, leading to an intense clash with the enemy. During the clash, Second Lieutenant Rahim Baloch, alias Aajiz Baloch, son of Dad Karim and a resident of Gomazi, made history through his bravery. He employed a strategic manoeuvre to ensure the safe passage of his comrades, standing his ground against the enemy and keeping them engaged while fighting with immense courage. This enabled his companions to safely escape the enemy's perimeter before he embraced martyrdom and became immortalised in history.
Aajiz Baloch joined the national struggle through the platform of the Balochistan Liberation Front in 2017. Initially, he made significant contributions to critical intelligence-based operations on the urban front. In 2021, he formally transitioned to the difficult and challenging life of guerrilla warfare in the mountains. Due to his exceptional combat skills and outstanding performance across various military fronts in Gomazi, Tump, Mand, Dasht, and Buleida, as well as his role in capturing enemy camps and establishing blockades to halt enemy movements, the organisation promoted him to the rank of Second Lieutenant. Because of his exceptionally gentle manner, kindness, and humble nature, Sangat Aajiz Baloch held a unique place among his comrades. These qualities earned him the organisational name “Aajiz.”

Ghulam Hussain Baloch (Saba Dashtyari) (2 September 1953 - 1 June 2011), from a low income Baloch family that had migrated from Iranian occupied Balochistan to Karachi, was a professor of Islamic studies and theology at the University of Balochistan in Quetta. Holding a master's degree in philosophy and Islamic studies from the University of Karachi, Dashtyari taught liberally despite personal atheistic views, fostering open discussions among students on progressive topics and Baloch identity. His scholarly and literary output included poetry, short stories addressing Baloch socioeconomic hardships - such as Aas o Aseeb and Tranagani bonzah - and broadcasts for Radio Quetta promoting the Balochi language since 1982; in 2003, he founded the Syed Hashmi Reference Library in Karachi to preserve Balochi texts and initiated certificate courses in the language. In later years, Dashtyari engaged in activism, criticizing Pakistan's policies toward Balochistan as colonial assimilation, advocating for the release of enforced disappearance victims through hunger strikes and seminars, and reportedly endorsing armed struggle for Baloch independence. He was assassinated by unidentified gunmen who shot him repeatedly on Sariab Road in Quetta while walking home, an attack unclaimed by any group but alleged by Baloch activists to involve Pakistani state genocidal forces amid a documented pattern of over 150 targeted killings of intellectuals, activists, and others in the province that year. No thorough independent investigation followed, despite international calls for accountability.

Early life and education
Family background and upbringing

Saba Dashtyari, born Ghulam Hussain Baloch, entered the world on September 2, 1953, in a lower middle class Baloch family residing in the slums of Lyari district, Karachi, Pakistan. His family had migrated from the Dashtiyari area of Iranian occupied Balochistan and their modest circumstances reflected the challenges faced by many in the Baloch diaspora, who had settled in urban centers like Karachi seeking economic opportunities amid Pakistan's post partition upheavals. From an early age, Dashtyari was immersed in Baloch cultural traditions within Karachi's diverse ethnic mosaic, where the community maintained linguistic and folk heritage despite pressures of assimilation into Urdu dominant urban life. This environment instilled resilience, as Baloch families navigated poverty and marginalization while preserving oral histories and poetry central to their identity. A pivotal early influence was exposure to Balochi literary giants, notably Banok Dashtyari, whose works sparked Dashtyari's affinity for Baloch language and folklore, laying the groundwork for his lifelong commitment to ethnic cultural continuity. Growing up in such surroundings honed his intellectual curiosity, fostering a worldview attuned to humanism and resistance against cultural erosion.

Formal education and influences

Dashtyari earned a master's degree in philosophy and Islamic studies from the University of Karachi. In 1979, he commenced doctoral studies but deferred completion upon securing a lecturing position at the University of Balochistan, prioritizing practical intellectual dissemination over advanced formal credentials. His linguistic proficiency spanned English, Persian, Arabic, Urdu, and Balochi, facilitating engagement with diverse scholarly traditions from Western philosophy to classical Islamic texts and regional poetry. This multilingual foundation supported self-directed exploration beyond institutional curricula, allowing synthesis of empirical reasoning with theological inquiry.Intellectually, Dashtyari drew from Baloch humanists like Syed Zahoor Shah Hashmi, a linguist and progressive thinker, whose emphasis on cultural preservation and rational critique shaped his integration of Islamic scholarship with secular humanism and poetic expression. Such influences underscored his independent pursuit of truth oriented philosophy, favoring causal analysis over dogmatic adherence.

Academic career.
Teaching positions and roles.

Dashtyari began his teaching career at Haji Abdullah Haroon School in Karachi, following his master's degrees in Islamic studies and philosophy. He subsequently joined the University of Balochistan in Quetta as a lecturer in Islamic Studies around 1979, advancing to the position of professor. Throughout his academic tenure from the late 1970s, Dashtyari maintained a commuting routine between his Karachi residence and Quetta, where he fulfilled his university obligations despite the logistical challenges of the 600 kilometer distance. This arrangement allowed him to sustain ties to his urban base while committing to instructional duties in Balochistan's primary public university. Although he initiated a PhD program in 1979, Dashtyari prioritized his lecturing role at the University of Balochistan over full-time doctoral pursuits, effectively forgoing completion to engage directly

On 13th April 2026, in the Barkhan area of Balochistan, Pakistani forces shelled and bombed civilian populations, killing twelve innocent Baloch civilians, including women and children, and seriously injuring three others.

The martyrs are:

- Ali, son of Sultan Umair, aged 40
- Babul, daughter of Gulzar, aged 30
- Mir Jan, son of Ali, aged 2
- Somri, daughter of Bhangan, aged 35
- Balach, son of Sabzo, aged 70
- Shari, aged 22
- Rehman, son of Balach, aged 18
- Naikho, daughter of Jamalan, aged 17
- Allah Bakhsh, son of Balach, aged 6
- Saddo, daughter of Balach, aged 13
- Hapo, daughter of Balach, aged 8
- Mahrang, daughter of Balach, aged 2

The injured are:

- Zarbibi, daughter of Sher, aged 55
- Hazar Khan, son of Balach, aged 9
- Israr, daughter of Balach, aged 15

This is not the first time that Pakistani forces have bombed civilians in Balochistan, targeting unarmed and innocent women and children as a form of collective punishment. Nor can this be considered “collateral damage.” Rather, the Pakistani state and its forces are deliberately targeting the Baloch people to maintain an atmosphere of fear in the region, suppress internal dissent, exploit Baloch coastal resources, and continue policies of genocide against the Baloch nation.

On 11 October 2026, a statement issued by Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) spokesperson Gwahram Baloch announced the martyrdom of 14 fighters of the organization who attained martyrdom in confrontations with the Pakistani army and in airstrikes while defending their homeland, Balochistan, and fighting for national liberation and the right to self-determination.

On 13 August 2026, Pakistani Air Force fighter jets bombarded the Pandran area of Kalat District in Balochistan, resulting in the martyrdom of four members of the organization: Waseem Baloch, alias Farhan; Obaidullah Baloch, alias Shaheen; Nawaz Ali Baloch, alias Dilshad; and Mohammad Hassan, alias Ahmad.

On 25 August 2026, during an organizational mission in the Kech area of Balochistan, Sher Jan, alias Jamal, was shot from behind by a traitor, resulting in his martyrdom.

On 3 September 2026, while patrolling in the Mastung area of Balochistan, the organization’s brave fighters, Mohammad Younis, alias Salal; Sameer Ahmad, alias Zemal; Aziz Ahmad, alias Janan; and Sikandar Baloch, confronted Pakistani forces, targeted several enemy personnel, and embraced martyrdom.

On 14 September 2026, while engaging Pakistani forces and defending his fellow fighters in the Machani Kor Paroom area of Panjgur District, Babar Baloch, alias Kambar, embraced martyrdom.

On 18 September 2026, during a confrontation with Pakistani forces in the Chagi area of Balochistan, fighters of the organization, Riaz Baloch, alias Sabir; Taimoor Shah, alias Shaheen; Zia Ul Haq, alias Ziaullah; and Jumma Baloch, alias Commando, embraced martyrdom.

Zia ul Haq, alias Ziaullah, son of Mohammad Tawan, resident of Chagi, joined the BLF in 2026. Having served the nation during guerrilla warfare in Chagi, Shaheed Ziaullah fought the enemy fiercely in the battle of Aminabad on 18 September 2026 and sacrificed his life for the homeland.

Karima Baloch was born on 4 February 1986 in the United Arab Emirates, where her parents, Mehrab Khan and Bibi Jamila, had moved from their native town of Tump prior to the rise of the modern Baloch national struggle. Despite spending her early years abroad, the love of her homeland pulled her back to Balochistan. After returning, she completed her early education at Tump Girls High School, then completed her intermediate studies (FSc) at Tump Inter College. She later enrolled at Atta Shad Degree College in Turbat, where she completed her graduation.

From a young age, Karima possessed a remarkable understanding of political processes, criticism, and administration. She was aware of the complexities of Baloch politics and was distinguished by her clear vision, confidence, and determination. Realizing the strength of her own abilities, she chose politics as her path and formally entered the political arena in 2006 by joining the Baloch Students Organization (BSO-Azad). In the same year, she became a member of the Central Committee, marking the beginning of a transformative journey in Baloch student politics. Her dynamic political presence challenged the perception that revolutionary movements were limited to male participation. She inspired Baloch women to join the struggle and proved that women could play a decisive role in national resistance.

This was also a time when the Pakistani state intensified enforced disappearances, targeting children, women, activists, and people from all walks of life. Coming from a revolutionary family, Karima understood the dangers she would face. Despite the constant threat of arrest, disappearance, and death, she never retreated. Her commitment remained unwavering: guiding the Baloch nation toward freedom, regardless of the price.

In 2008, during the council session at the University of Balochistan in Quetta, Karima made history by becoming the Junior Vice Chairperson of BSO-Azad, the first woman to hold such a high-ranking position in the organization. Her leadership continued to rise; in 2012, during the Awaran Council Session, she was elected Senior Vice Chairperson. Her responsibilities grew even further in 2014 when the Chairman of BSO-Azad, Zahid Baloch, was forcibly disappeared by Pakistani forces and intelligence agencies. As vice chairperson, Karima had to carry the full weight of organizational leadership during one of the most difficult periods in BSO-Azad’s history. She worked tirelessly day and night to keep the organization active and united.

In 2015, after nearly a decade of uninterrupted political struggle, Karima was elected as the Central Chairperson of BSO-Azad, becoming the first woman in Baloch history to lead the organization.

Her activism extended beyond Balochistan. In 2016, Karima Baloch was included in the BBC’s list of the 100 most influential and inspirational women in the world. Her work focused on educating and politicizing the Baloch nation, raising awareness of enforced disappearances, state violence, and the occupation of Balochistan. She organized and led protests, hunger strikes, seminars, and awareness campaigns to expose human rights violations committed by Pakistani forces. Her activism also drew international attention to the Baloch cause.

At the end of 2015, BSO-Azad decided to send her to Canada so she could further mobilize the international community and strengthen global support for the Baloch struggle.

Tragically, on 20 December 2020, Karima Baloch was assassinated by Pakistani state-backed elements in Toronto, Canada. Her body was found the next day on a Toronto island. Her martyrdom triggered widespread grief and anger across Balochistan and the global Baloch diaspora. Massive protests erupted in Karachi, Quetta, Turbat, and towns across Balochistan, as well as internationally. Slogans echoed everywhere: How many Karimas will you kill? Every home will become Karima Baloch. I am Karima, you are Karima, we are all Karima.

Karima Baloch was brought back to her homeland and laid to rest in Tump. Her martyrdom cemented her place as one of the most iconic symbols of Baloch resistance. She was not only a leader of the Baloch nation but also a voice for oppressed people globally. Her courage, dedication, and sacrifice continue to inspire generations, making her a timeless symbol of defiance and national dignity.

Sattar Baloch, son of Ghulam Qadir, was born in 1988 in Khuzdar. He received his early education in his native area and was a student of engineering at the Balochistan University of Engineering and Technology, Khuzdar. He was a member of BSO Azad, Khuzdar Zone. He played a key role in mobilizing the Baloch youth of his surrounding areas to join the Baloch liberation movement.
He had a keen interest in reading revolutionary literature. He believed in political struggle and was targeted for exercising peaceful political activities. He was threatened by security agencies to quit BSO Azad, but he remained in the movement until the end.
He was a victim of target killing by personnel of Pakistan’s intelligence agencies on 11 June 2010 in Khuzdar district, Balochistan. He was killed for exercising his basic right to engage in politics. His body showed extreme signs of torture. He was among the most committed members of the organization and continued his struggle during difficult times. He inspired many youths to join the caravan of BSO Azad.
His sacrifices for the independence of the Baloch homeland at a very young age will be remembered in golden words in the chapters of Baloch history.

Martyr Mukhtar Baloch, alias Kunar Baloch, was a resident of the Balor Kolwa area of Kech, Balochistan. He was affiliated with the Baloch Republican Army (BRA) for several years. He embraced martyrdom during a military clash with the Pakistan Army in the Kolwa area of Kech on October 25, 2020.

data.organization: Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) / Saddo Operational Battalion (SOB)
data.biography:
The fighters of the Balochistan Liberation Front’s special unit, the Saddo Operational Battalion (SOB), attacked the Brigade Headquarters in the Nokundi area of Chagai, Balochistan, at around 8:19 PM on the night of November 30, 2025. SOB fighters successfully entered the offices and residential compound of foreign employees of the Saindak and Reko Diq projects, located in the centre of the camp, and managed to take several foreigners present in the compound hostage. The Pakistani army deployed its air force, SSG commandos, and modern heavy weapons against the fighters, but the brave Sarmachars of SOB repelled every attempt and forced them to retreat. During the operation, the Balochistan Liberation Front offered the Pakistani side an opportunity to negotiate on its demands; however, 18 hours after the offer, the Pakistani army chose to use force and began directly targeting the compound with artillery and aerial attacks. This resulted in intense clashes between the occupying forces and the fighters, which continued until the martyrdom of the SOB fighters.
In this special operation by the Saddo Operational Battalion, 76 military personnel, including foreign hostages, were killed, and 6 SOB fighters embraced martyrdom. The Nokundi operation by SOB was a continuation of the BLF’s long-standing armed resistance strategy for the independence of Balochistan and the protection of its natural wealth.
Among the martyrs were:
1 Asif alias Khalid Baloch, son of Mulla Ghulam Jan.
2 Inayat Sahil alias Gwahram Baloch, son of Ishaq Baloch.
3 Zareena Rafiq alias Tranag Maho, daughter of Master Rafiq Ahmed.
4 Nabeel Ahmed alias Ustad Adil Baloch, son of Haji Muhammad Ishaq.
5 Meer Jan Meeral alias Janan Baloch, son of Muhammad Raheem Baloch.
6 Ghulam Jan alias Istaal Baloch, son of Faiz Muhammad.
Fighter Zareena Rafiq, alias Tranag Maho, daughter of Master Rafiq Ahmed and a resident of Singabad Karki Tijaban, joined the BLF in 2022. In 2024, she offered her services to the Saddo Operational Battalion. By participating in this significant mission, she became the first female Jind Nadr (self-sacrificer) of the BLF.
On 30 November 2025, Zareena Baloch carried out a suicide attack on the entry barriers of the main compound of the Nokundi Brigade Headquarters. By detonating the gates and barriers of the compound, she sacrificed her life for the Baloch national cause and paved the way for her fellow fighters to enter the Brigade Headquarters and reach the residential compound of foreign employees working on the Reko Diq and Saindak projects.
The success of the operation was made possible only by Zareena Baloch’s exemplary bravery, courage, and spirit of sacrifice.

On 25 August 2024 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch announced the launch of a "Fidayeen Operation" named "Herof" across Balochistan. As part of this operation, fidayeen from the BLA's elite unit, Majeed Brigade, have attacked the main camp of the Pakistani forces in Bela and have successfully infiltrated it. Meanwhile, other BLA fighters have taken full control of all major highways across Balochistan, blocking them completely.
During Operation “Herof,” 44 attacks were carried out simultaneously at 40 locations across 13 districts of Balochistan. As a result, 130 Pakistani army personnel were killed and 55 were injured. In addition, gas pipelines were destroyed at 2 locations, railway tracks at 7 locations, and 2 bridges were blown up.
During the operation, 13 vehicles transporting minerals were set on fire. Blockades were also established at 14 locations across Balochistan, and 3 members of a “death squad” were killed.
As part of the Baloch Liberation Army’s fidayee (suicide) operation “Herof,” the BLA’s Majeed Brigade carried out an attack on the Pakistani army’s Bela camp. The Majeed Brigade maintained control of the camp for twenty hours, during which 68 enemy personnel were killed.
Nine fidayeen (self-sacrificing fighters) of the Majeed Brigade at Bela camp - Ghaus Bakhsh Sumalani (alias Talib), Mahal Baloch (alias Zilan Kurd), Rizwan Baloch (alias Hammal), Mohammad Baloch (alias Meerak), Fazal Gul Zehri (alias Shawaiz), Tayyab Baloch (alias Lala), Junaid Zehri (alias Kami), Mohammad Asif Nechari (alias Naveed), and Mohammad Bakhsh Sumalani (alias Khalid) - along with Shafqat (alias Dayar) of the Fateh Squad in Mastung, were martyred in the operation.
Ghaus Baksh Sumalani, alias Talib, and Mohammad Bakhsh Sumalani, alias Khalid, were brothers. They took part in the same operation and were martyred while defending their motherland.

On 22 July 2026, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) released the details of seven martyred members of the organization: Abdul Ghafoor, alias Chakar, son of Jan Mohammad; Imdad Baloch, alias Nodh, son of Rahmatullah; Hafiz Mumtaz Baloch, alias Zeerak, son of Sabir Ali; Hafiz Zaid Baloch, alias Sagaar, son of Mullah Khudadad; Yasir Baloch, alias Ajiz, son of Mohammad Ayub; Shahjan Baloch, alias Sawad, son of Ali Mohammad; and Ali Raza Baloch, alias Shayhaq, son of Haji Ali Ahmad. They were martyred in a drone strike by Pakistani forces on 29 January 2026 in the Pardan area of Panjgur District, Balochistan.

Yasir Baloch, alias Ajiz, son of Mohammad Ayub, was a resident of the Washbod area of Panjgur. He joined and served in the Urban Front in 2021, and in 2023, he moved to the Mountain Front in Panjgur, where he was killed on 29 January 2026 in Pardan, Panjgur.
Yasir Baloch, alias Ajiz, remained associated with the Baloch Liberation Army for five years. During this period, he carried out the organization's responsibilities in different areas to the best of his ability. He began his involvement as an urban guerrilla and worked continuously in that role for two years. During this time, he monitored the enemy's activities within the city and provided assistance to his fellow fighters in countering those activities. After spending two years on the urban front, he joined the mountain front in 2023 on the directives of the organization, entered the organizational camp, and completed his basic military training courses.
He carried out the responsibilities assigned to him by the organization at different times on the Kilkor, Gichk, and Panjgur fronts. Alongside his fellow Sarmachars, he remained an organized force in the region. In addition to protecting people's lives and property from the enemy, he consistently raised awareness among them about national freedom and the importance of an independent Baloch state. Together with his fellow fighters, he worked to strengthen and expand the organization's presence in these areas. He was among the fighters involved in attacks carried out against the enemy in the respective areas. While Ajiz was considered a formidable opponent by the enemy, he was also a supportive companion to his fellow Sarmachars.
He continued his armed struggle against the enemy until his final moments and was killed in a drone strike in January of this year while fighting against the occupying forces. The sacrifices he made will be remembered in history, and they will ultimately contribute to the pursuit of a free and sovereign Balochistan.

In 1838, the British sent a force led by Alexander Burnes to reinstate Shah Shuja Durrani as the king of Afghanistan by deposing Amir Dost Mohammad Khan. To reach Afghanistan, they needed passage through Balochistan, particularly the Bolan Pass. However, Khan Mehrab Khan refused to allow the British to use his land to attack a neighboring country. The British sent Lieutenant Leach to negotiate with the Baloch government, but the Khan stood firm. When British forces reached Shaal via Bolan, some patriotic Baloch, without the Khan’s knowledge, attacked British troops out of nationalist sentiment and a desire to protect their homeland.
After toppling Amir Dost Mohammad Khan, the British Governor General of India, Lord Auckland, ordered an attack on Balochistan. In 1839, around 7,000 British troops marched from Shaal to attack the Baloch Meeri (capital). Anticipating an invasion, Khan Mehrab Khan declared war and sent messages to tribal leaders, but many saw the British as allies rather than invaders and chose to collaborate with them rather than defend their land. When Khan Mehrab Khan gathered his resistance fighters, the number of loyal warriors had dwindled to only 700 due to the short sightedness of many tribal chiefs. Nevertheless, Mehrab Khan was determined to fight. At his court, a respected figure, Akhund Muhammad Siddiq, advised him that he was not in a position to wage war at that time. He suggested that the Khan should leave Kalat with his companions, regroup and strengthen his forces, and then launch an attack against the British when the time was right, on 13 November 1839, the British forces launched an attack on Kalat, and a fierce battle ensued. During the fighting, Khan Mehrab Khan Baloch was martyred by a British bullet.

At 5:00 AM on 31 January 2026, Jeeyand Baloch, spokesperson for the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), issued a statement announcing the commencement of the second phase of Operation Herof against the occupying state and its military and administrative structures. The operation remained active for six days, concluding at 4:00 PM on 6 February 2026.
On 6 February 2026, a concluding statement by the spokesperson declared that Operation Herof Phase 2 had concluded in a decisive victory across all fronts. It stated that Operation Herof Phase 2, carried out by the Baloch Liberation Army, was a six-day campaign of coordinated urban combat and represented the most extensive, intense, and organized military engagement in the modern history of the Baloch national resistance. The operation, which began at 5:00 AM on 31 January and ended at 4:00 PM on 6 February, successfully achieved its strategic objectives. Fourteen cities across Balochistan were targeted. Baloch fighters launched simultaneous attacks and established effective control over numerous enemy posts, military installations, and urban sectors. In several cities, BLA units maintained uninterrupted dominance over occupying forces for six consecutive days, inflicting significant political, psychological, and military damage on the enemy.
During the operation, 93 BLA fighters were martyred. These included 50 fidayeen from the Majeed Brigade, 26 fighters from the Fateh Squad, and 17 from the Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS). All major BLA units participated in the operation, including Majeed Brigade, STOS, Fateh Squad, ZIRAB (intelligence wing), and Hakkal (media wing). Over 362 enemy personnel were killed, including members of the Pakistani Army, Frontier Corps, police, and state-sponsored death squads. Seventeen enemy soldiers were captured. Ten, identified as Baloch, were released with warnings, while seven remained in BLA custody and faced trial for war crimes and acts of genocide.
On 14 February 2026, another statement by the spokesperson announced that the seven occupying army personnel were in custody and that a one-week prison of war exchange had been offered. The Pakistani Army ignored the offer and intensified its military operations. On 3 March 2026, a subsequent statement declared that, due to misadventures and breaches of promises by the occupying forces, death sentences were carried out against the seven Pakistani personnel.
During Operation Herof Phase 2, dozens of Pakistani military facilities were destroyed, weapons stockpiles were seized, and the unified, disciplined resistance dealt a substantial blow to the military superiority of the occupying state.
During Operation Herof Phase 2, the BLA’s Majeed Brigade Fidayeen targeted the main camp and the Coast Guard camp of the Pakistan Navy in the coastal city of Pasni, Balochistan. The operation was initiated by Fazal, alias Miraan, who rammed a vehicle loaded with explosives into the main entrance gate of the Navy camp. The explosion instantly killed at least seven personnel stationed at the gate.
Immediately after this initial attack, six Fidayeen - Yasma Baloch, alias Zareena; Waseem Baloch, alias Zirbaar; Zaid Zamurani, alias Abram; Sabzal Baloch, alias Kohsar; Diljan Baloch, alias Ameer Ajoo; and Operation Commander Shabeer Baloch, alias Kiya - entered the camp and took up positions. Fierce clashes with the occupying Navy and Navy special units inside the camp continued for more than five hours, during which at least 33 Pakistani personnel were killed. This operation not only inflicted significant casualties on the enemy but also dealt a severe blow to the defense structure of the Navy camp.
Diljan Baloch, alias Ameer Ajoo, son of Dil Murad, was born in 2005 and was a resident of Sar Dasht, Kulanch, Tehsil Pasni, District Gwadar. He joined the Baloch Liberation Army on 1 November 2023 and became part of the Majeed Brigade in February 2024. He was martyred while fighting on the Pasni front.
Those who stood beside him remember a young fighter defined by composure under pressure and clarity of purpose. He carried his responsibilities quietly, without display, remaining steady in the most difficult moments. His martyrdom on the Pasni front marked the end of a life lived with resolve and the fulfillment of a path he had consciously chosen.

Imam Baloch, son of Mohammad Ilyas, was a 22-year-old laborer and resident of Shaban Bazaar, Mand, Kech. He was taken into custody, along with his brother, Mohammad Omar, by the Frontier Corps on 10 July 2026 near Balicha Keras while they were returning home. Both were allegedly extrajudicially killed on the same day without being charged with any crime or given an opportunity to defend themselves.
Later that day, the bodies of Imam Baloch and his brother, Mohammad Omar, were handed over to their family bearing gunshot wounds.

Fida Ahmad Baloch was an intellectual, linguist, ideologist and political leader whose wisdom and vision inspired generations. His motto, “Unity and struggle till the final victory,” remains a guiding slogan for every Baloch.

Born in 1957 in Turbat, Fida dedicated his life to the cause of a free and greater Balochistan. From his early days in BSO (Awami) to his efforts in uniting Baloch student movements, he exemplified courage and conviction. Even after knowing he was marked as a target, he never abandoned his struggle. On 2 May 1988, he was martyred when armed men opened fire inside his own bookshop in Turbat.

On 13 October 2026, Pakistani genocidal forces killed six Baloch men who had previously been subjected to enforced disappearance and dumped their bodies in the Sui area of Dera Bugti district, Balochistan.
The incident was also confirmed by Sher Mohammad Bugti, the Central Spokesperson of the Baloch Republican Party.

The victims have been identified as follows:
- Mohammad Khan Bugti, son of Yar Mohammad Bugti
- Lalu Bugti, son of Taj Mohammad Bugti
- Shahmeer Bugti, son of Shahal Bugi
- Waheed Bugti, son of Habib Bugti
- Ghulam Din Bugti, son of Kurri Bugti
- Akram Khan, son of Wadera Mazar Khan Bugti

On 17 May 2019, a statement issued by the spokesperson of the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) said that two BLA fighters and one fighter of the Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) were killed in combat with the Pakistan Army and its affiliated death squad, which operates under the supervision of Qambar Khan, in the Kalat area of Balochistan on Thursday, 16 May 2019.
Qambar Khan is a local tribal chief in the Parod area of Kalat and the son of a well-known Baloch freedom fighter, the late Lawang Khan, who was killed by the Pakistani Army during the insurgency in Balochistan in the 1970s.
According to locals and pro-freedom organizations, Qambar Khan is now working with the Pakistan Army and has formed a death squad in the area to fight against Baloch freedom fighters. Several skirmishes between BLA fighters and Qambar Khan’s death squad have also been reported in the past.
The BLA spokesperson said, “Several Pakistani forces personnel and affiliates of Qambar Khan were killed in the combat, during which two BLA fighters, Mama Shams Pirkani Baloch and Doctor Shoaib Baloch alias Gazain, along with a Balochistan Liberation Front fighter, Zafar Mohammed Hasni alias Khuddal, embraced martyrdom.”

On February 10, 2011, two mutilated bodies were found in Heronk, 40 kilometres from Turbat city. They were identified as Abdul Qayum Baloch and Jameel Yaqoob Baloch. Abdul Qayyum Baloch, son of Nazar Mohammad Baloch age 38 was a Central Committee member of the Baloch Student Organization (BSO-Azad), who was abducted on December 11, 2010, by the Pakistani army from his house in Gwadar. For 61 days, his whereabouts remained unknown until the discovery of his body. He was a staunch pro-independence activist and very vocal against the Pakistan government’s policy of bringing demographic changes to Balochistan through its Gwadar deep-sea port project. His agitation against the port, along with other activists, brought international media attention to Gwadar.
Jameel Yaqoob Baloch, son of Mohammad Yaqoob age 34, a member of the Balochistan National Party (BNP-Mengal), was abducted by the Pakistani army on August 28, 2010, from Turbat. He was a labourer, working on daily wages to support his family. In life, these activists advocated different ideologies for the betterment of their beloved nation: Shaheed Abdul Qayum Baloch supported freedom, while Shaheed Jameel Yaqoob Baloch campaigned for self-determination. In death, their sacred blood mingled in the soil of their motherland and spoke with one voice: “We were tortured and killed because we are Baloch; our ideology does not matter to them.”
Faisal Rodeni, was a resident of the Kalat area of Balochistan. He was martyred on 10 May 2013 in Balochistan.

The fighters of the Balochistan Liberation Front’s special unit, the Saddo Operational Battalion (SOB), attacked the Brigade Headquarters in the Nokundi area of Chagai, Balochistan, at around 8:19 PM on the night of November 30, 2025. SOB fighters successfully entered the offices and residential compound of foreign employees of the Saindak and Reko Diq projects, located in the centre of the camp, and managed to take several foreigners present in the compound hostage. The Pakistani army deployed its air force, SSG commandos, and modern heavy weapons against the fighters, but the brave Sarmachars of SOB repelled every attempt and forced them to retreat. During the operation, the Balochistan Liberation Front offered the Pakistani side an opportunity to negotiate on its demands; however, 18 hours after the offer, the Pakistani army chose to use force and began directly targeting the compound with artillery and aerial attacks. This resulted in intense clashes between the occupying forces and the fighters, which continued until the martyrdom of the SOB fighters.
In this special operation by the Saddo Operational Battalion, 76 military personnel, including foreign hostages, were killed, and 6 SOB fighters embraced martyrdom. The Nokundi operation by SOB was a continuation of the BLF’s long-standing armed resistance strategy for the independence of Balochistan and the protection of its natural wealth.
Among the martyrs were:
1 Asif alias Khalid Baloch, son of Mulla Ghulam Jan.
2 Inayat Sahil alias Gwahram Baloch, son of Ishaq Baloch.
3 Zareena Rafiq alias Tranag Maho, daughter of Master Rafiq Ahmed.
4 Nabeel Ahmed alias Ustad Adil Baloch, son of Haji Muhammad Ishaq.
5 Meer Jan Meeral alias Janan Baloch, son of Muhammad Raheem Baloch.
6 Ghulam Jan alias Istaal Baloch, son of Faiz Muhammad.
Inayat Sahil alias Gwahram Baloch, son of Ishaq Baloch, resident of Soleer Gichak, was assigned as second commander in the operation of Nokundi. Inayat Sahil Baloch joined BLF in 2017 and volunteered for Saddo Operational Battalion in 2023. He played an exemplary role as second-in-command in the success of the operation, demonstrating excellent military capabilities. He was great marksman and an expert of modern weapons. Inayat Baloch embraced martyrdom on December 2 in SOB's operation.

data.biography:
On February 4, 2026, in the Turbat area of Balochistan, armed goons of a death squad operating as a proxy for Pakistani forces shot and killed Balach Khalid.
Balach had previously been taken into custody by Pakistani forces on October 25, 2023 and was forcibly disappeared. He was later handed over to the notorious so called Counter Terrorism Department. He had also survived two prior assassination attempts.
In the local language 'death squad' refers to armed groups that operate directly under the command of Pakistani forces and, in return, are granted full freedom by them to commit all kinds of crimes.

data.biography:
On 16 October 2026, a statement issued by the Baloch Republican Guards (BRG) stated that, on the night of 30 September 2026, occupying Pakistani forces arrived in the Sunni area of Kachhi district, Balochistan, to conduct an operation. A sudden confrontation took place between the occupying forces and the freedom fighters, who launched a deadly attack against the enemy. As a result, the occupying army suffered significant casualties and material losses.

During the clashes, five devoted BRG freedom fighters - Bafa Jan Jatoi, son of Lal Jan Jatoi, a resident of Sunni, Kachhi; Fareed Jan Jatoi, alias Zahri, son of Ghulam Jan, a resident of Sunni, Kachhi; Obaidullah Jan Jatoi, son of Sajjar Khan, a resident of Sunni, Kachhi; Imam Din Jatoi, alias Mumtaz, son of Nihal Khan, a resident of Sunni, Kachhi; and Ayaz Jan Ghola, alias Alim, son of Abdul Sattar, belonging to the Ghola Baloch tribe and a resident of Sunni, Kachhi - embraced martyrdom while defending their homeland and fighting for national independence.

All these freedom fighters were highly dedicated, brave, hardworking, and disciplined comrades. They inflicted various forms of losses on the occupying enemy in several areas of Balochistan, including Kachhi, Dhadar, Sunni, Bolan, and Sibi.
